description: Learn how to add metadata to your pages and create dynamic OG images.
related:

  description: Learn more about the Metadata APIs mentioned in this page.

---

The Metadata APIs can be used to define your application metadata for improved SEO and web shareability and include:

1. [The static `metadata` object](#static-metadata)
2. [The dynamic `generateMetadata` function](#generated-metadata)
3. Special [file conventions](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata) that can be used to add static or dynamically generated [favicons](#favicons) and [OG images](#static-open-graph-images).

With all the options above, Next.js will automatically generate the relevant `<head>` tags for your page, which can be inspected in the browser's developer tools.

The `metadata` object and `generateMetadata` function exports are only supported in Server Components.

## Default fields

There are two default `meta` tags that are always added even if a route doesn't define metadata:

- The [meta charset tag](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTML/Element/meta#attr-charset) sets the character encoding for the website.
- The [meta viewport tag](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTML/Viewport_meta_tag) sets the viewport width and scale for the website to adjust for different devices.

```html
<meta charset="utf-8" />
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1" />
```

The other metadata fields can be defined with the `Metadata` object (for [static metadata](#static-metadata)) or the `generateMetadata` function (for [generated metadata](#generated-metadata)).

## Static metadata

To define static metadata, export a [`Metadata` object](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-metadata#metadata-object) from a static [`layout.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/layout) or [`page.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page) file. For example, to add a title and description to the blog route:

```tsx filename="app/blog/layout.tsx" switcher
import type { Metadata } from 'next'

export const metadata: Metadata = {
  title: 'My Blog',
  description: '...',
}

export default function Layout() {}
```

```jsx filename="app/blog/layout.js" switcher
export const metadata = {
  title: 'My Blog',
  description: '...',
}

export default function Layout() {}
```

You can view a full list of available options, in the [`generateMetadata` documentation](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-metadata#metadata-fields).

## Generated metadata

You can use [`generateMetadata`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-metadata) function to `fetch` metadata that depends on data. For example, to fetch the title and description for a specific blog post:

```tsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx" switcher
import type { Metadata, ResolvingMetadata } from 'next'

type Props = {
  params: Promise<{ slug: string }>
  searchParams: Promise<{ [key: string]: string | string[] | undefined }>
}

export async function generateMetadata(
  { params, searchParams }: Props,
  parent: ResolvingMetadata
): Promise<Metadata> {
  const slug = (await params).slug

  // fetch post information
  const post = await fetch(`https://api.vercel.app/blog/${slug}`).then((res) =>
    res.json()
  )

  return {
    title: post.title,
    description: post.description,
  }
}

export default function Page({ params, searchParams }: Props) {}
```

```jsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/page.js" switcher
export async function generateMetadata({ params, searchParams }, parent) {
  const slug = (await params).slug

  // fetch post information
  const post = await fetch(`https://api.vercel.app/blog/${slug}`).then((res) =>
    res.json()
  )

  return {
    title: post.title,
    description: post.description,
  }
}

export default function Page({ params, searchParams }) {}
```

### Streaming metadata

For dynamically rendered pages, Next.js streams metadata separately, injecting it into the HTML once `generateMetadata` resolves, without blocking UI rendering.

Streaming metadata improves perceived performance by allowing visual content to stream first.

Streaming metadata is **disabled for bots and crawlers** that expect metadata to be in the `<head>` tag (e.g. `Twitterbot`, `Slackbot`, `Bingbot`). These are detected by using the User Agent header from the incoming request.

You can customize or **disable** streaming metadata completely, with the [`htmlLimitedBots`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/htmlLimitedBots#disabling) option in your Next.js config file.

Prerendered pages don’t use streaming since metadata is resolved at build time.

title: favicon, icon, and apple-icon
description: API Reference for the Favicon, Icon and Apple Icon file conventions.
---

The `favicon`, `icon`, or `apple-icon` file conventions allow you to set icons for your application.

They are useful for adding app icons that appear in places like web browser tabs, phone home screens, and search engine results.

There are two ways to set app icons:

- [Using image files (.ico, .jpg, .png)](#image-files-ico-jpg-png)
- [Using code to generate an icon (.js, .ts, .tsx)](#generate-icons-using-code-js-ts-tsx)

## Image files (.ico, .jpg, .png)

Use an image file to set an app icon by placing a `favicon`, `icon`, or `apple-icon` image file within your `/app` directory.
The `favicon` image can only be located in the top level of `app/`.

Next.js will evaluate the file and automatically add the appropriate tags to your app's `<head>` element.

| File convention             | Supported file types                    | Valid locations |
| --------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | --------------- |
| [`favicon`](#favicon)       | `.ico`                                  | `app/`          |
| [`icon`](#icon)             | `.ico`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.png`, `.svg` | `app/**/*`      |
| [`apple-icon`](#apple-icon) | `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.png`                 | `app/**/*`      |

### `favicon`

Add a `favicon.ico` image file to the root `/app` route segment.

```html filename="<head> output"
<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico" sizes="any" />
```

### `icon`

Add an `icon.(ico|jpg|jpeg|png|svg)` image file.

```html filename="<head> output"
<link
  rel="icon"
  href="/icon?<generated>"
  type="image/<generated>"
  sizes="<generated>"
/>
```

### `apple-icon`

Add an `apple-icon.(jpg|jpeg|png)` image file.

```html filename="<head> output"
<link
  rel="apple-touch-icon"
  href="/apple-icon?<generated>"
  type="image/<generated>"
  sizes="<generated>"
/>
```

> **Good to know**:
>
> - You can set multiple icons by adding a number suffix to the file name. For example, `icon1.png`, `icon2.png`, etc. Numbered files will sort lexically.
> - Favicons can only be set in the root `/app` segment. If you need more granularity, you can use [`icon`](#icon).
> - The appropriate `<link>` tags and attributes such as `rel`, `href`, `type`, and `sizes` are determined by the icon type and metadata of the evaluated file.
> - For example, a 32 by 32px `.png` file will have `type="image/png"` and `sizes="32x32"` attributes.
> - `sizes="any"` is added to icons when the extension is `.svg` or the image size of the file is not determined. More details in this [favicon handbook](https://evilmartians.com/chronicles/how-to-favicon-in-2021-six-files-that-fit-most-needs).

## Generate icons using code (.js, .ts, .tsx)

In addition to using [literal image files](#image-files-ico-jpg-png), you can programmatically **generate** icons using code.

Generate an app icon by creating an `icon` or `apple-icon` route that default exports a function.

| File convention | Supported file types |
| --------------- | -------------------- |
| `icon`          | `.js`, `.ts`, `.tsx` |
| `apple-icon`    | `.js`, `.ts`, `.tsx` |

The easiest way to generate an icon is to use the [`ImageResponse`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/image-response) API from `next/og`.

---
name: storyfolio
description: Use when someone wants a personal portfolio site made from their profile, resume, LinkedIn or GitHub, especially one with 3D, scroll-driven animation or a story, or says their portfolio looks generic, templated or AI-made.
---

# Storyfolio

Makes one kind of portfolio site: one long scroll that introduces the person in 3D, each chapter's scene a picture of what it is about.

Start from the recorded handover on a continuation. For a requested build, sketch concepts at stop 2; build the chosen site after storyboard approval. A planning-only request still ends at the storyboard.

## Stops

Between stops you work by yourself. At each stop the person decides one thing. You go on only when their answer is in the conversation and you have written it into the file.

| Stop | First open | You put to the person | You go on when |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Read | `references/reading-a-profile.md` | What you found, as facts to confirm and questions to answer. No concept or design | They have answered, and `docs/story/facts.md` holds their answers |
| 2. Concept | `references/concept.md` | Three concepts, runnable for a requested build, and which you would choose | They have picked one, or told you to pick, and `docs/story/concepts.md` says which |
| 3. Storyboard | `references/storyboard.md` | The script of the whole page | They have said yes to it |
| 4. Spine | `references/building.md`, `engine/README.md` | A runnable opening, middle and ending in two or three looks | They have chosen a look |
| 5. Chapters | `references/building.md` | The remaining chapters and three whole-beat wording versions | They have chosen the wording |
| 6. Finish | `engine/README.md` | The checked site and what still needs their review | Their actual review is recorded |

**When starting from profile material, your first reply is the first stop, and no more than that.** Brief build-setup notes do not advance the design. People ask for the whole plan at once: the idea, the scroll, the colours. Do not give it yet, and say why in a sentence. A plan made now is made from your reading of a resume, and a resume leaves out exactly what a site must not get wrong: whose result a number was, what a title hides, who took a photograph. Once they have answered you will have a better idea, and it will not have to be taken apart.

## Ask or decide

Ask the person when a thing is:

1. a fact only they know,
2. a claim that could embarrass them if it were wrong,
3. taste on what a visitor sees first: the concept, the look, the opening words,
4. anything that publishes, costs money, or shows another person or an employer's work.

Everything else you decide. Write each decision into `docs/story/decided-for-you.md`: what you decided, why, and how to change it.

If the person will not answer, or tells you to decide everything, open `references/asking.md`.

## What you keep

In the person's own folder, so that a later session can go on from the files alone:

| File | Holds |
|---|---|
| `docs/story/facts.md` | The fact sheet, each fact with where it came from, and the person's answers |
| `docs/story/concepts.md` | The three concepts, which was picked, and why |
| `docs/story/storyboard.md` | The script |
| `docs/story/decided-for-you.md` | What you decided without asking |
| `docs/story/handover.md` | What exists, what the person has said, what is next |

## What holds from the first stop on

- **Nothing about the person is invented.** You know that a number, an employer, a title and a quote are facts. So is every small thing a sentence says on its way: what was wrong before they came, how often a thing is used, which came first, why, how a thing was left, what it taught them. That sounds like writing, and it is a claim. Before handing over any reply or file, check each claim against the fact sheet, including introductory summaries, working titles and words in the scene. Read the supporting line and its unresolved questions, not just its reference. It must establish the whole claim: a topic attached to one item does not establish the topic of another. Wording that depends on an unanswered question stays out of the introduction and the planned page, even if copied from a profile. Remove it or list it as a question to confirm. An illustration of the kind of thing they work with, labelled as one, claims nothing: a plated dessert, a status page. A particular design, a measured value or an event does. An empty scene is no safer.
- **A number is used as the person confirmed it,** with what it measures and whose result it is.
- **What is someone else's is asked about before it is planned for:** a photograph a photographer took, a friend's drawing, a quote, an employer's screens, a story with a patient or a client in it.
# Building

## The spine and its look

Build the opening, one middle chapter and the ending in two or three looks.
Let the person scroll those looks, ask which they choose, and stop for their
answer before building the remaining chapters. An unanswered question in
this turn is not a refusal to choose or permission to choose for them.

## The chapters and their words

After the look choice, build the remaining chapters. For the opening and
closing wording, show three versions of each whole beat, including the
surrounding fixed text. Recommend one and leave room for their own wording.
Stop for the choice, then use it word for word.

## The scene

Compare the running scene with the storyboard at its settled beats. With the captions hidden, does each scene show what the storyboard says it shows, rather than only names for it? Revise the composition when the explanation lives only in the surrounding prose. Keep that accessible prose; it does not replace what the scene was meant to show.

Inspect the changes between beats in both scroll directions, including intermediate positions. When words in the scene change, correct any overlap that makes the old and new words unreadable together. A readable settled beat does not establish a readable transition.

Read every word in the scene at the size it is shown on a desktop, a phone and a short screen. Words too small to read there go to the caption.
